newsitem.title: TURKEY: BSEC looks to Turkey business meeting for progress.
newsitem.headline: BSEC looks to Turkey business meeting for progress.

text.p: The Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC) grouping will hold a business conference in Istanbul next month which it hopes will finally convert nearly four years of planning into concrete projects.

"For the first time in Istanbul we will put together some specific projects," said Nihat Gokyigit, president of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation Business Council, of the Black Sea region business conference, scheduled for April 28-30.

"BSEC did not come up with many specific projects so far," Gokyigit told reporters. "It has been busy trying to put its organs into operation. That is done at last, and the Black Sea Trade and Development Bank will open in Thessaloniki in May."

The Turkish governor of the bank, seen as the locomotive for the group, said last week that it was set to start operations in May following delays due to a lack of financial contribution from member states, many of whom are in dire financial straits.

Some heads of state, ministers of transport, economy and communication, representatives of the World Bank, the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development and the International Finance Corporation, and some 600 businessmen are expected to attend the Istanbul conference.
BSEC, the brainchild of former Turkish president Turgut Ozal, was set up in June 1992 in Istanbul amid hopes over Ankara's leadership potential in the region.

The grouping has a secretariat in Istanbul, a parliamentary assembly, the private-sector business council and an economic data centre and several working bodies, but it has not undertaken any projects so far.
Business council secretary-general Mustafa Aksin acknowledges the BSEC's shortcomings in its efforts to boost regional trade and economic cooperation.
"During the last four years the organs of the group were developed and that took some time," he said. "Concrete results will be more discernible in the future, but they will be there."

Aksin said another factor slowing the progress of BSEC was the lack until now of a private sector in most members -- the group comprises Turkey, Greece, Moldova, Albania, Bulgaria, Romania, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Ukraine and Russia.
Bilateral antagonism between member countries and the troubled economies of ex-Soviet states have not helped matters.
But despite the initial problems, Aksin said he hoped there would be a free trade zone in the region by 2010.
Gokyigit said the conference aimed to develop projects in telecoms, power, agroindustry, transport and the environment.
